items.name: Readability
items.evidence: The final /app/run.py content isn't in the log. The tested drafts it came from (steps 21-22) use clear names (tasks_list, queue, worker, task_fn), typed signatures and a typed asyncio.Queue. I found no cryptic names in business logic.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: A single short coroutine with a nested worker, built on asyncio.Queue plus TaskGroup. It is a little more involved than the semaphore approach but still compact. The exploratory scripts with prints ran only as python3 -c and were not left in run.py.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: It raises ValueError("max_concurrent must be positive") and returns early on an empty list. TaskGroup provides structured cancellation and awaits each task's cleanup. Tests showed cleanup running on both SIGINT and cancel, and no exceptions are swallowed.

items.name: Failures and degenerate arguments
items.evidence: Empty list returns at once and max_concurrent<=0 raises ValueError. In step 16 a failing task produced an ExceptionGroup and the sibling cleanup ran (cleaned_up: [0, 1]). Queued items are never pulled once TaskGroup cancels the workers.

items.name: Required signature and import behaviour
items.name_zh: 签名与导入行为符合要求
items.evidence: async def run_tasks(tasks: list[Callable[[], Awaitable[None]]], max_concurrent: int) -> None. Workers call each callable only after taking it from the queue, so it runs only when a slot is free. Stdlib only, and the import test in step 24 passed.
